prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Management by Trajectory (MBT) Concept of Operations (ConOps) implements Trajectory Based Operations (TBO), consistent with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) guidance, across National Airspace System (NAS) Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) operations. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), airspace users/operators, aircraft, pilots, controllers, traffic managers and automation participate. FAA/users negotiate assigned closed four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs), current-state-to-destination. Aircraft comply within tolerances and share predicted intent. Controllers retain separation responsibility; routine self-separation is not assumed. Automation supports proactive clearances/multisector coordination; changes reach affected users, aircraft and FAA automation. NAS Constraint Service publishes static/dynamic constraints; traffic management automation translates traffic management initiatives (TMIs) into traceable flight-specific constraints. Negotiating controllers subsume D-side responsibilities; traffic management coordinators (TMCs) support traffic flow management (TFM). Near-term: mixed equipage, System Wide Information Management (SWIM) extensions. Far-term: widespread Aeronautical Telecommunications Network-Baseline 2 (ATN-B2), digital trajectory receipt, known tracking accuracy, automatic/manual Flight Management System (FMS) loading; voice retained. Electronic flight bags (EFBs) gain broadband. Required Time of Arrival (RTA) FMS supports one active RTA; controller-pilot data link communications (CPDLC) exchanges clearances/intent. Traffic Collision Avoidance System/Airborne Collision Avoidance System (TCAS/ACAS), Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) detect-and-avoid and Advanced Interval Management (A-IM) evolve toward coordinated tactical avoidance; aircraft transmit maneuvers to ground automation. Ground Delay Programs (GDPs)/Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) shift toward Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA). Time-Based Flow Management (TBFM) expands en-route, addressing airspace/airport constraints; generic miles-in-trail (MIT) restrictions disappear. Without metering, time-based management/A-IM provides spacing. MBT supports distance/time-based separation. Required Time Performance (RTP) complements Required Navigation Performance (RNP): RTP-Y denotes crossing-time-error 95% confidence interval, seconds, regardless of distribution shape, for TOAC constraints. All aircraft require RTP certification, even without RTA. Flight operations centers, applications/private providers enable participation. NAS accommodates on-demand/personal mobility, UAS, space launch/return, airships/loitering. Scope:

New part:
U0086: Therefore, the application of MBT to surface operations will not be pursued in this effort unless the incremental benefits of including management of surface operations within the MBT concept is justified.
U0087: Application of TBO elements is still possible without the full application of MBT to surface operations.
U0088: For example, the ATM system can plan and control pushback times based on scheduled takeoff times and with consideration of runway queue management, without needing to provide a closed trajectory on the surface.
U0089: However, MBT is compatible with TBO concepts that do envision a closed trajectory on the surface such as [3].
U0090: What is most important for MBT, from the surface point of view, is exchange of the necessary data to provide an interface between surface and en route operations and an assigned trajectory that is consistent with a surface management plan that delivers expected surface event times that impact airborne operations [1].
U0091: For example, reliable takeoff and landing time predictions, runway assignments, and inclusion of the departure and arrival transitions in the assigned trajectory support coordination between en route and surface environments.
U0092: Surface operations will be very diverse for different types of users, further motivating treating MBT ground operations as a separate research topic.
U0093: Emergent users may share traditional airports or operate to/from alternative sites.
U0094: Space vehicles operate from special launch and recovery sites and often have no surface movements.
U0095: Rotorcraft are able to “air taxi” and therefore are not constrained by taxiways and do not require runways. 1.6.2 Traffic Flow Management Traffic flow management is separate from the MBT concept.
U0096: TFM is responsible for selecting traffic management initiatives (TMIs), which impose constraints on trajectories.
U0097: The MBT concept addresses the assignment of trajectories that are compliant with all TMIs, the modification of assigned trajectories as constraints change, and the satisfaction of the constraints as aircraft follow the assigned trajectories.
U0098: Improved predictability resulting from MBT will allow TFM to select more-effective TMIs.
U0099: In the near-term, GDPs and AFPs will continue to function as they presently do.
U0100: In the longer-term environment, GDPs/AFPs will move from controlling through the use of an Expect Departure Clearance Time (EDCT) constraining the departure time to enforcement of the CTA at the limited resource as a time constraint on the assigned trajectory.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
